items.prompt: What makes a decision a 'multi-criteria decision,' in this unit's sense?
choices: Several distinct, hard-to-compare factors all bear on which option is best, with no single number capturing all of them
Any decision that happens to take more than one meeting of discussion to finally resolve
A decision where exactly one single factor is uncertain, like a future cost estimate
A decision that happens to be made collaboratively by more than one person at once
items.explanation: A multi-criteria decision isn't defined by how long it takes or how many people are involved -- it's defined by having several genuinely different factors (risk, cost, maintainability, etc.) that can't be collapsed into one another.
items.reference:
📏 several criteria, none reducible to the others
⚖️ weights say how much each one counts

Why: A multi-criteria decision has no single number that captures every factor -- naming the criteria and weighing them explicitly is what makes a structured comparison possible at all.

items.prompt: Priya, Marcus, and Dana are each arguing for a different priority (deploy velocity, operational risk, onboarding speed). Why does this count as a multi-criteria decision rather than three people just disagreeing about facts?
choices: Because each of them is prioritizing a genuinely different, non-interchangeable factor -- the disagreement is about weighting, not about what's true
Because they're simply arguing too loudly in the same meeting room at the same time, drowning each other out
Because none of them has actually bothered to read the product roadmap carefully before the meeting
Because the decision hasn't actually been made yet, despite three weeks of meetings
items.explanation: None of them is factually wrong about their own priority mattering. The disagreement is about how much each factor should count relative to the others -- exactly the shape of a multi-criteria decision.
items.reference:
📏 several criteria, none reducible to the others
⚖️ weights say how much each one counts

Why: A multi-criteria decision has no single number that captures every factor -- naming the criteria and weighing them explicitly is what makes a structured comparison possible at all.

items.prompt: What does it mean for two criteria to be 'incommensurable,' as used in this unit?
choices: They can't be converted onto a common scale -- operational risk isn't 'worth' some exact number of onboarding-weeks
They're both automatically equally important by definition, regardless of context
One of them must be a mistake, since real criteria always reduce to cost in the end
They can never both be scored on the same 1-10 numeric scale under any circumstances
items.explanation: Incommensurable criteria are genuinely different kinds of things -- there's no exchange rate between operational risk and onboarding speed the way there is between two amounts of money. That's why they need weights, not a conversion formula.
items.reference:
📏 several criteria, none reducible to the others
⚖️ weights say how much each one counts

Why: A multi-criteria decision has no single number that captures every factor -- naming the criteria and weighing them explicitly is what makes a structured comparison possible at all.

choices: They're actually the same underlying problem at heart, just given two different names in two different units of this curriculum
They're actually the same underlying problem, just given two different names in two different units
expected-value only ever applies to purely financial decisions, while this unit only ever applies to purely technical ones
This unit is really just expected-value applied three separate times in a row to different factors
items.explanation: expected-value is about probability-weighting the possible outcomes of a single dimension. This unit is about weighing several different dimensions -- cost, risk, maintainability -- none of which collapse into a single probability-weighted number.
items.reference:

⚖️ weights say how much each one counts

Why: A multi-criteria decision has no single number that captures every factor -- naming the criteria and weighing them explicitly is what makes a structured comparison possible at all.

items.prompt: A teammate says 'let's just convert operational risk into a dollar cost and add it to the budget, then it's a single-number decision.' What's the issue with that move?
choices: It's sometimes possible with real effort, but often forces a fake precision onto a factor that was never truly a dollar amount -- collapsing incommensurable criteria doesn't remove the judgment call, it hides it
It's always the correct and only valid approach to take with any multi-criteria decision you could ever possibly face in practice
Operational risk can never, under any circumstances whatsoever, be expressed in any numeric form at all, full stop
This is exactly what a weighted-scoring matrix already does by itself, so there's no meaningful difference at all
items.explanation: Forcing every criterion into one unit doesn't eliminate the underlying judgment call about how much risk 'costs' -- it just buries that judgment call inside a conversion rate instead of keeping it visible as an explicit weight.
items.reference:

⚖️ weights say how much each one counts

Why: A multi-criteria decision has no single number that captures every factor -- naming the criteria and weighing them explicitly is what makes a structured comparison possible at all.

items.prompt: What is a 'weight,' as this unit uses the term?
choices: A number expressing how much a given criterion should count relative to the others, made explicit rather than left as an unstated personal priority
The raw 1-10 score that a single option happens to get on just one particular criterion in the matrix, nothing more than that
The total number of criteria that were identified by the group as relevant to the decision at hand
A synonym for 'the correct answer,' used interchangeably once the matrix has finally been built
items.explanation: A weight isn't a score for an option -- it's how much a criterion counts, period, regardless of which option is being evaluated. Scores and weights are different numbers doing different jobs.
items.reference:
🤷 unstated priorities look like disagreement about the decision
📝 named priorities look like disagreement about one weight

Why: Writing criteria and weights down turns a shapeless argument into a specific, resolvable disagreement about a single number.

No -- they were each arguing from pure, objective fact with no personal judgment involved at all
Yes, but only Marcus actually had a real priority; the other two were just being difficult
items.explanation: Each of them already had an implicit weighting in their head -- the problem wasn't the absence of weights, it was that the weights were silent and unstated, so the group was arguing about the conclusion instead of the actual point of disagreement.
items.reference:

items.prompt: What is 'sensitivity analysis,' in the context of a multi-criteria decision?
choices: Re-checking whether a decision's top-scoring option still wins under other reasonable weightings, instead of trusting the first one tried
A survey that simply asks employees how they personally feel about a given decision after it's made
A one-time calculation that never needs to be repeated once a first weighting is chosen
A synonym for the word 'weight,' used interchangeably with it throughout this unit
items.explanation: Sensitivity analysis is specifically about testing robustness -- rerunning the scoring under several plausible weightings to see whether the same option keeps winning, or whether the first result was fragile.
items.reference:
🔁 rerun scoring under 2-4 other plausible weightings
🏆 same winner every time -> robust
🔀 winner flips -> the number was one guess, not a signal

Why: A recommendation built on only the first weighting anyone tried is trusting one person’s judgment call more than it deserves.

items.prompt: What does 'tie-breaker judgment' mean in this unit, and when does it apply?
choices: Deciding on factors like reversibility or who bears the cost of being wrong, used when two options score too close together for the numeric gap to be a reliable signal
Flipping a coin whenever two options happen to score uncomfortably close together on the matrix
Always just deferring automatically to whichever person has the most seniority in the room, regardless of their actual stake
A step that replaces the weighted-scoring matrix entirely, used instead of it from the very start
items.explanation: Tie-breaker judgment is specifically for the close-call case -- when the score gap is thin enough that it isn't a trustworthy signal, the decision should turn on reversibility, who bears the cost, or what would be regretted more, not on squeezing more precision from noisy inputs.
items.reference:
🔁 rerun scoring under 2-4 other plausible weightings
🏆 same winner every time -> robust
🔀 winner flips -> the number was one guess, not a signal

Why: A recommendation built on only the first weighting anyone tried is trusting one person’s judgment call more than it deserves.

items.prompt: In the weighted-scoring matrix mechanic, what are the three steps in order?
choices: List options and assign criteria weights, score every option per criterion, compute each option's weighted score (sum of score x weight)
Score every option first on gut feel, then decide only afterward what the criteria even are
Pick a winner purely by gut feeling first, then build a matrix afterward just to justify it
Assign weights first, then discard whichever criteria scored lowest before doing any actual scoring
items.explanation: The order matters: criteria and weights are decided before scoring options, so the scoring isn't biased by already knowing which option a given weighting would favor.
items.reference:
1️⃣ list options and criteria, assign weights
2️⃣ score every option per criterion
3️⃣ weighted score = sum of (score × weight)

Why: The matrix combines several incommensurable criteria into one comparable number per option -- not a measurement, a structured combination of judgment calls.

items.prompt: In the matrix, why should the weights for all criteria sum to a fixed total, like 1.0?

It's purely an arbitrary stylistic convention here that has no real effect on the final computed result
It's purely an arbitrary stylistic convention that has no real effect on the final result
So that every option automatically ends up with the same final weighted score
items.explanation: A fixed total makes weights comparable to each other -- 0.30 out of 1.0 clearly means 'the largest single factor,' whereas an unconstrained set of weights loses that shared reference point.
items.reference:
1️⃣ list options and criteria, assign weights
2️⃣ score every option per criterion
3️⃣ weighted score = sum of (score × weight)

Why: The matrix combines several incommensurable criteria into one comparable number per option -- not a measurement, a structured combination of judgment calls.

items.explanation: Each criterion's contribution is its own score times its own weight, and the contributions are added -- not multiplied together, and not summed before weighting.

3️⃣ weighted score = sum of (score × weight)

The arithmetic coming out correct automatically guarantees that the original criteria list was already complete
Once computed for this one decision, weights no longer need reviewing again for any future decision at all
items.explanation: Careful arithmetic doesn't upgrade the nature of its inputs. A weighted score is exactly as reliable as the honesty and care behind the weights and scores that produced it -- no more.

3️⃣ weighted score = sum of (score × weight)

It guarantees that the chosen option is, in fact, objectively the best possible one available to choose
items.explanation: The matrix's value isn't manufacturing objectivity -- it's converting vague disagreement into a specific, arguable claim about one number, which is exactly what let L1's stuck meeting resolve in twenty minutes.

items.prompt: A sensitivity check shows the same option winning under three plausible reweightings. Is this the same kind of guarantee as a passing automated test?

items.prompt: In `weightedScore(option, weights)`, why does the reduce walk `Object.keys(weights)` rather than `Object.keys(option.scores)`?

items.explanation: Walking the weights' keys means the function only accumulates contributions from criteria that were actually assigned a weight -- an unweighted score sitting in `option.scores` correctly contributes nothing.

📊 rankOptions: sorts options by that score, highest first

items.prompt: A compliance requirement nobody had weighed at all surfaces three weeks into a multi-criteria decision. What's the correct way to incorporate it into the existing sensitivity analysis?
choices: Treat it as a reason to restart weighting from scratch, since every existing weight was implicitly calibrated against an incomplete criteria list, not patch the old weight sets with the new criterion bolted on
Simply add the new criterion to the options' scores only, leaving every one of the existing weight sets completely and totally unchanged
Ignore it entirely, since sensitivity analysis is only ever meant to handle weight disagreement, never new criteria
Give the new criterion a weight of exactly 0 so that it doesn't disturb any of the existing results in any way
items.explanation: Every existing weight was chosen relative to the old, incomplete list of criteria -- silently adding a new criterion without redoing the weighting understates it unevenly across options, which is worse than admitting the whole weighting needs revisiting.
items.reference:
➕ new criterion mid-decision -> restart weighting, don’t patch old weight sets
🔢 disagreement about a raw score -> find better evidence, not more weightings

Why: A weight dispute and a score dispute are different kinds of disagreement, and conflating them is a common way this framework gets misused.

items.prompt: Marcus rates 'extract 2 services now' a 5 on operational risk; an SRE who ran the last migration insists it's a 2. Does rerunning sensitivityAnalysis with different weight sets resolve this disagreement?
choices: No -- sensitivityAnalysis only varies weights while holding scores fixed, so a disagreement about a raw score needs better evidence about that score (like incident history), not more reweighting
Yes -- adding enough additional weight sets always eventually resolves any disagreement, including disagreements about raw scores
No, because scores can never legitimately be disputed once they've already been entered into the matrix at all
Yes, because scores and weights are really just interchangeable numeric inputs to the exact same scoring function
items.explanation: A weight dispute and a score dispute are different problems. sensitivityAnalysis as built only tests robustness to weight changes -- resolving a disagreement about the actual 1-10 score requires finding who has the stronger evidence, not running more weightings.

items.prompt: Complete `weightedScore(option, weights)`. It should return the sum, over every criterion key present in `weights`, of `option.scores[criterion] * weights[criterion]`.

tests.expr: expect(weightedScore({ scores: { operationalRisk: 8, teamFamiliarity: 9, maintainability: 4, timeToValue: 9, cost: 8 } }, { operationalRisk: 0.30, teamFamiliarity: 0.25, maintainability: 0.20, timeToValue: 0.15, cost: 0.10 })).toBe(7.6)

tests.description: a single-criterion weighting returns score times weight

items.explanation: Object.keys(weights) walks only the weighted criteria, and reduce accumulates score times weight for each one. Starting the accumulator at 0 means an empty weighting correctly contributes nothing.
items.reference:
🧮 weightedScore: sum of (score × weight) per criterion
📊 rankOptions: sorts options by that score, highest first

Why: Object.keys(weights).reduce(...) walks every criterion once, multiplying and accumulating -- the same arithmetic as the by-hand matrix in L2, just executable.

items.prompt: The starter `weightedScore` below has a bug: it multiplies every score by the *same* weight instead of that criterion's own weight. Fix it so each criterion uses its own weight from the `weights` object.

tests.expr: expect(weightedScore({ scores: { operationalRisk: 8, teamFamiliarity: 9, maintainability: 4, timeToValue: 9, cost: 8 } }, { operationalRisk: 0.30, teamFamiliarity: 0.25, maintainability: 0.20, timeToValue: 0.15, cost: 0.10 })).toBe(7.6)

expect(weightedScore({ scores: { operationalRisk: 5, teamFamiliarity: 5, maintainability: 9, timeToValue: 4, cost: 4 } }, { operationalRisk: 0.30, teamFamiliarity: 0.25, maintainability: 0.20, timeToValue: 0.15, cost: 0.10 })).toBe(5.55)

tests.description: differently-weighted criteria no longer collapse to the same contribution
tests.expr: expect(weightedScore({ scores: { a: 10, b: 0 } }, { a: 0.9, b: 0.1 })).toBe(9)

items.explanation: The bug used the first weight found for every criterion, which silently collapses a multi-criteria matrix into a single-weight one -- every criterion needs its own weights[criterion] lookup, not one shared value.

items.prompt: Complete `topTwoGap(options, weights)`. Using the already-available `weightedScore` function, rank the options by weighted score (highest first) and return the numeric gap between the 1st and 2nd place scores.

tests.description: baseline weighting: gap between stay-monolith and extract-now is 2.05
tests.expr: expect(topTwoGap([{ name: 'a', scores: { c: 8 } }, { name: 'b', scores: { c: 3 } }], { c: 1 })).toBe(5)

tests.description: a three-option field still compares only the top two
tests.expr: expect(topTwoGap([{ name: 'a', scores: { c: 10 } }, { name: 'b', scores: { c: 7 } }, { name: 'c', scores: { c: 1 } }], { c: 1 })).toBe(3)

tests.description: a tie produces a gap of 0
tests.expr: expect(topTwoGap([{ name: 'a', scores: { c: 5 } }, { name: 'b', scores: { c: 5 } }], { c: 1 })).toBe(0)

items.explanation: Mapping every option to its weighted score, sorting descending, and subtracting the second entry from the first gives exactly the top2Gap sensitivityAnalysis reports -- the number that separates a comfortable win from a thin, judgment-call-required one.
items.reference:
🔁 rerun scoring under 2-4 other plausible weightings
🏆 same winner every time -> robust
🔀 winner flips -> the number was one guess, not a signal

Why: A recommendation built on only the first weighting anyone tried is trusting one person’s judgment call more than it deserves.

items.prompt: Complete `winnerHoldsAcrossAll(options, weightSets)`. Given an array of `{ label, weights }` objects, return `true` if the same option wins under every weight set, `false` if the winner ever differs.

tests.description: same winner under two weight sets returns true
tests.expr: const opts = [{ name: 'a', scores: { c: 9, r: 1 } }, { name: 'b', scores: { c: 1, r: 1 } }]; expect(winnerHoldsAcrossAll(opts, [{ label: 'x', weights: { c: 1, r: 0 } }, { label: 'y', weights: { c: 0.9, r: 0.1 } }])).toBe(true)

tests.description: a flipped winner under one weight set returns false
tests.expr: const opts = [{ name: 'a', scores: { c: 9, r: 1 } }, { name: 'b', scores: { c: 1, r: 9 } }]; expect(winnerHoldsAcrossAll(opts, [{ label: 'x', weights: { c: 1, r: 0 } }, { label: 'y', weights: { c: 0, r: 1 } }])).toBe(false)

tests.description: a single weight set trivially holds
tests.expr: const opts = [{ name: 'a', scores: { c: 5 } }, { name: 'b', scores: { c: 2 } }]; expect(winnerHoldsAcrossAll(opts, [{ label: 'only', weights: { c: 1 } }])).toBe(true)

items.explanation: Collecting the winning name under every weight set and checking they're all equal to the first is exactly what 'robust under sensitivity analysis' means in code -- one flipped entry anywhere in the list makes the whole check false.

🏆 same winner every time -> robust
